name: Chinese Poker
description: Chinese Poker (also known as Pusoy, Russian Poker, or 13 Cards) is a card game where players arrange 13 cards into three poker hands (back, middle, front) that must increase in strength. Players compare hands against each other to win units. Popular in Hong Kong, Southeast Asia, and the USA.
alsoKnownAs: Luosong Pai Jiu 羅宋牌九

history.origins:
Country/Region of Origin: China/Hong Kong
Time Period: Traditional game, popularized in 20th century
Historical Development: Known as Sap Sam Cheung (十三張 - 13 cards) in Cantonese. Also called Luosong Pai Jiu (羅宋牌九 - Russian Pai Gow) in Chinese. Distantly related to Pai Gow.
Cultural Significance: Popular gambling game in Hong Kong, Southeast Asia, and among Asian communities in the USA.
timeline: Traditional origins: Played for generations in China
20th century: Popularized in Hong Kong and Southeast Asia
Modern Era: Spread to USA, particularly Hawaii (called Pepito) and Filipino communities (called Pusoy)
Recent development: Open Face Chinese Poker variant created
history.cultural: Known by many names across different regions: Pusoy (Philippines), Pepito (Hawaii), Russian Poker, Good Better Best. The game is often played for money with agreed unit values.
history.evolution: The traditional game evolved into Open Face Chinese Poker, where hands are built face up one card at a time after the initial five cards. This variant has become popular in poker player circles.

rules.objective: Arrange 13 cards into three poker hands (back: 5 cards, middle: 5 cards, front: 3 cards) where back ≥ middle ≥ front in strength. Win units by beating opponents' corresponding hands.
rules.gameplay: Each player receives 13 cards and arranges them into three hands face down: back hand (5 cards, strongest), middle hand (5 cards, middle strength), front hand (3 cards, weakest). Back must beat middle, middle must beat front. Players expose hands simultaneously. Each pair of players compares corresponding hands, winning one unit per hand beaten.
keyRules: Arrange into back (5), middle (5), front (3) hands
Back hand must be strongest, then middle, then front
Front hand: only 3-of-a-kind, pair, or high card possible
Straights and flushes don't count in front hand
Win 1 unit per hand beaten against each opponent
Foul (mis-set) hands lose all three hands to all opponents

strategy.basic: Ensure your hands are legal (back ≥ middle ≥ front). Put your strongest hand in back, weakest in front. Don't risk fouling by making front too strong.
strategy.intermediate: Balance hand strength across all three positions. Consider that front hand only needs to beat other front hands - don't over-commit strong cards there. Look for opportunities to make three of a kind in front for bonus. Manage risk of fouling versus potential rewards.
strategy.advanced: Sophisticated hand arrangement considering probabilities of opponents' holdings. Optimal distribution of pairs and high cards. Recognizing when to play for sweep (winning all three hands). Understanding expected value of different arrangements. In Open Face, tracking exposed cards and adjusting strategy.
tips: Never foul - ensure back ≥ middle ≥ front
Front hand only needs to beat other fronts - conserve strength
Three of a kind in front is valuable (3 units)
Consider probability of opponents having certain hands
Balance risk of strong middle versus weak back
Special hands (six pairs, three straights) are automatic winners
In Open Face, watch opponents' exposed cards carefully

scoring.description: Basic scoring: Win 1 unit for each corresponding hand you beat, lose 1 unit for each hand that beats you. Special hands: Three of a kind in front wins 3 units instead of 1. Full house in middle wins 2 units. Four of a kind in back/middle wins 4 units. Royal/straight flush in back/middle wins 5 units. Special 13-card hands win automatically: Six pairs (3 units), Three straights (3 units), Three flushes (3 units), Complete straight A-K (13 units).
